## My data

My fairness dataset is the Adult Income Dataset. One row is one person, with 5000 total rows. My sports dataset is the Marathon Race Results Dataset. One row is one runner, with 26598 total rows.

#| label: data

## Part A · Fairness

### A0 · See it update

```{r}
#| label: fig-a0

```

Yes, the updated title appeared in the report and slides.

### A1 · Label it

```{r}
#| label: fig-a1
#| ref.label: a1
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Share of each group with the outcome, labeled for a reader."
#| fig-alt: "A stacked bar chart showing the percentage of people above and below $50K in each education group."
```

```{r}
#| label: a1-check
#| include: false
```

I changed the x-axis label the most because I wanted to make it clear that the percentages represent income categories within each education group. I think a reader could understand the plot without an explanation because the title, axes, and legend describe what is being compared.

### A2 · Choose a scale

```{r}
#| label: fig-a2
#| ref.label: a2
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "My scale choice."
#| fig-alt: "A histogram showing the distribution of positive capital gains using a logarithmic x-axis."
```

```{r}
#| label: a2-check
#| include: false
```

I used a logarithmic scale for capital gain because most values are small, while some are much larger. Compared with a linear scale, the log scale makes the differences among smaller positive values easier to see. I excluded 4563 zero or negative values because they cannot be displayed on a logarithmic scale.

### A3 · Facet it: fixed or free

```{r}
#| label: fig-a3
#| ref.label: a3
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "The same rates in panels: fixed and free y-axes."
#| fig-subcap: ["Fixed", "Free"]
#| fig-alt: "Two faceted bar charts comparing the percentage earning above $50K across education levels and sex categories, using fixed and free y-axis scales."
#| layout: [[1, 1]]
```

```{r}
#| label: a3-chosen
#| include: false
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-a3
#| tbl-cap: "Each group's n and rate, by panel."
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(a3_rates, digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: a3-check
#| include: false
```

I chose fixed scales because they make it easier to compare income percentages between the panels. The reader gains a consistent scale for comparison, but smaller differences within a panel may be harder to see than with free scales. The percentages vary across education levels and between the sex categories. The smallest education-by-sex group, which is preschool-female, has only one observation, so its percentage should be interpreted cautiously.

### A4 · Compared to what?

```{r}
#| label: fig-a4
#| ref.label: a4
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Two groups: individual values and resampled means, same axes."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels comparing individual capital gains and resampled mean capital gains for bachelor's degree holders and high school graduates."
```

```{r}
#| label: a4-check
#| include: false
```

The individual values show considerable overlap between the two education groups, with many people having little or no capital gain. The resampled means show how much the average could vary between samples. Comparing the panels helps distinguish differences between individual people from differences between group averages.

### A5 · Color for every reader

```{r}
#| label: fig-a5
#| ref.label: [a5, a5-simulated]
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "My colors, with a second cue, and how a reader with red-green color blindness might see them."
#| fig-subcap: ["My plot", "Red-green (deuteranopia), simulated"]
#| fig-alt:
#|   - "A bar chart showing the number of people at each education level, separated into panels by sex and distinguished using a viridis color scale."
#|   - "The same plot in the colors a reader with red-green color blindness (deuteranopia) might see."
#| layout-ncol: 2
```

```{r}
#| label: a5-colors
#| echo: true
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-a5-views
#| ref.label: a5-other-views
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "The other two simulated views."
#| fig-subcap: ["Red-green (protanopia), simulated", "Blue-yellow (approximate), simulated"]
#| fig-alt:
#|   - "The same plot in the colors a reader with red-green color blindness (protanopia) might see."
#|   - "The same plot in the colors a reader with blue-yellow color blindness might see (an approximation)."
#| layout-ncol: 2
```

```{r}
#| label: a5-check
#| include: false
```

I used the sex column for color because it has only a few categories, making the colors easier to distinguish. I chose a viridis color scale to improve accessibility for readers with color-vision differences. I also separated the categories into panels so readers do not have to rely on color alone. In the simulated views, the categories can still be identified using the panel labels.

## Part B · Sports

### B1 · Label it

```{r}
#| label: fig-b1
#| ref.label: b1
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "My Sports plot, labeled for a reader."
#| fig-alt: "A scatter plot showing runners' net finishing times across age groups, with colors representing gender."
```

```{r}
#| label: b1-check
#| include: false
```

The plot shows how runners' finishing times vary across age groups and gender categories. I think the y-axis label is the most helpful because it explains that finishing times are measured in minutes.

### B2 · Choose a scale

```{r}
#| label: fig-b2
#| ref.label: b2
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "My scale choice."
#| fig-alt: "A histogram showing the distribution of runners' overall finishing positions on a logarithmic scale."
```

```{r}
#| label: b2-check
#| include: false
```

I used a logarithmic scale for overall finishing position to display a wide range of ranks. This spreads out the lower ranks and compresses the higher ranks, making the earlier finishing positions easier to distinguish. No zero or negative finishing positions were removed.

### B3 · Facet it: fixed or free

```{r}
#| label: fig-b3
#| ref.label: b3
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "The same plot in panels: fixed and free y-axes."
#| fig-subcap: ["Fixed", "Free"]
#| fig-alt: "Two sets of boxplots comparing finishing times across age groups and gender categories, using fixed and free y-axis scales."
#| layout: [[1, 1]]
```

```{r}
#| label: b3-check
#| include: false
```

I chose fixed scales because they allow finishing times to be compared directly between the gender panels. The reader gains a consistent y-axis, although differences within each panel may be less noticeable than with free scales. The boxplots show how finishing times vary across age groups and gender categories. The smaller panel contains 11423 runners, which is important to consider when comparing the groups.

### B4 · Compared to what?

```{r}
#| label: fig-b4
#| ref.label: b4
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Two groups: individual values and resampled means, same axes."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels comparing individual finishing times and resampled mean finishing times for male and female runners."
```

```{r}
#| label: b4-check
#| include: false
```

The individual finishing times show variation within both gender groups, with runners from both groups having overlapping finishing times. The resampled means show how much the average finishing time could vary between samples. This helps distinguish differences between individual runners from differences between the group averages.

### B5 · Color for every reader

```{r}
#| label: fig-b5
#| ref.label: [b5, b5-simulated]
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "My colors, with a second cue, and how a reader with red-green color blindness might see them."

#| fig-alt:
#|   - "A horizontal bar chart showing the number of Boston Marathon runners in each gender category, using a viridis color scale."
#|   - "The same plot in the colors a reader with red-green color blindness (deuteranopia) might see."
#| layout-ncol: 2
```

```{r}
#| label: b5-colors
#| echo: true
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-b5-views
#| ref.label: b5-other-views

#| fig-cap: "The other two simulated views."
#| fig-subcap: ["Red-green (protanopia), simulated", "Blue-yellow (approximate), simulated"]
#| fig-alt:
#|   - "The same plot in the colors a reader with red-green color blindness (protanopia) might see."
#|   - "The same plot in the colors a reader with blue-yellow color blindness might see (an approximation)."
#| layout-ncol: 2
```

```{r}
#| label: b5-check
#| include: false
```

I used gender for the fill colors because it has only a few categories, making the colors easier to distinguish. I chose the viridis color scale to improve accessibility for readers with color-vision differences. I also put gender on the y-axis so readers can identify the categories without relying only on color. The categories remain identifiable in the simulated views because of the axis labels.

## One thing I tried in my slides, and why

I focused my slides on income differences across education levels and sex categories. I used the fixed-scale version of my A3 plot so readers could compare percentages between the panels without having to account for different axis ranges. I also organized the slides so the research question comes before the main finding and the limitations come afterward.
